title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
authors: Maor Ben Shahar, Jonathan Morag, Dirk Englund, Kfir Sulimany
abstract: Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.
summary: This work develops a novel, machine-verified framework in the Lean proof assistant to rigorously prove the security of Quantum Key Distribution protocols like BB84. By formalizing the entire process, including finite-size effects and LOCC constraints, the authors eliminate ambiguity in security assumptions. This establishes a reproducible, automated standard for security proofs in quantum cryptography.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of establishing end-to-end, machine-verified security theorems for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, specifically closing gaps in existing proofs due to mismatched assumptions.
main_result: The authors provide the first end-to-end, machine-verified composable finite-key security proof for the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks.
method: The core method involves formalizing the entire protocol and its security analysis within the Lean proof assistant, utilizing LLM-based autoformalization and a specialized Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC) language.
model_or_system: The focus is on the theoretical security analysis of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol, modeling quantum operations using Kraus maps and defining security via the diamond norm distance between real and ideal quantum channels.
key_observables: Security bound ($\epsilon_{	ext{QKD}}$), key rate (finite-size penalty), and the distinguishability between the real and ideal quantum channels.
important_parameters: Finite block size, coherence of attacks, and the robustness bound ($\delta_{	ext{rob}}$) related to the abort probability.
main_assumptions: The security proof is fundamentally built upon the assumption of Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the AI-assisted proving workflow (AI agents $	o$ Lean kernel checking $	o$ manual review). Figure 2 details the machine-checked BB84 development using the LOCC construction.
paper_structure: The paper develops a formal framework in Lean to model quantum protocols, applies this framework to the BB84 protocol to prove finite-key security, and discusses the integration of autoformalization pipelines to accelerate discovery.
why_interesting: It demonstrates a powerful synergy between theoretical quantum information security and advanced formal verification tools (Lean), setting a new standard for rigorously proving quantum protocols.
